Because I so often see the gaming aspect as the reason that someone won't make the switch to Linux, and while I don't always agree with their reasoning, I am sympathetic towards people that don't switch for financial/business/economic reasons, so I'm not going to get all purist on those type of people.

Honestly, I don't think this will cause "the year of Linux" (on the desktop). I work part-time at a computer shop; sooo many people truly don't care. They only get upset about being pestered by the update ads.

That said, I do think this will be good for Linux desktop. It will push that minority of people who do care to explore other options. It will not be a huge wave, but over the next few years as Windows 7 nears its end-of-life, a decent number of people will start exploring moving to Linux, dual-booting, getting comfortable with it. Combine that with Valve's push for gaming on Linux. Barring any major changes in Europe (hopefully Win10 will scare Europe badly enough for governments & consumers there to start ditching Windows in droves), by 2020 we might see Linux break 5% or (fingers crossed) maybe even 10% of desktop share. It will remain a distant competitor to Windows, but it will be on par with OSX; it will no longer be treated as a 2nd-class citizen (or as non-existent) by many software vendors, but too many big name software pieces will still not be ported for Linux to be viable for many categories of professionals. Dell might offer a few decent low & mid range consumer computers with Ubuntu pre-installed with a decent amount of success. But the majority of users will stay on Windows because changing is hard. Sure, you have to change from Win7 to Win10 & from Win10 to Win11 (Win10 Extended?) but Microsoft will Do That For YouTM because you can no longer choose not to. It will be easier for most to just give in and learn the new systems as Microsoft pushes them out.

In the next 5-10 years, Chrome OS (or its successor) will also gain, mostly at Windows' expense. It will stabilize somewhere between 10% & 20% of market share. It will lead to some improvements in software support for Linux, but mostly Google will try to keep everything in-house & online based. Windows will fall from the current ~85% to ~60% but Microsoft will be making scads of money via the ad business.

From there, we might see Linux begin to take off but we could also see ChinaSoft Doors sweep the market. Or IndiaPear Bartlett. Or some other OS from another (currently not-quite) developed nation.

TL;DR

Win10 will not cause Linux to take off, but it will give it a nice shove. Combine that with Valve's push for Linux, Chrome OS, and other possible factors, the OS market will become fairly fractured with Windows still at the top but significantly less so than today and Linux with a much larger but still minority share.
